title: CASE SCENARIO 14
passage_html: Karma Ltd. got incorporated in 1980s as a private limited company and started its business into two segments – printing and construction. The two business activities were completely different but those were managed very well and the company grew significantly over a period of time. In year 2001, the company got converted into a public company and in 2008, the company also got listed on Bombay Stock Exchange. The turnover of the company was increasing, however, the margins were not increasing as per the expectations of the management and the management analysed this aspect and realized that the margins were not so high in case of printing segment. The company decided to focus more on construction business and included infrastructure in its line of business. This was also because of the fact that the government policies were favourable towards the infrastructure sector. Eventually, the company decided to sell its printing segment in 2020. The new investor (i.e. buyer) for the printing segment carried out a due diligence of the printing business involving various aspects and the company sold this segment in January 2021. Since the business of the company included infrastructure and it involved transactions with government officials also, the management suspected certain suspicious transactions for which it decided to carry out forensic accounting in the financial year 2021-22. During the audit, certain transactions were identified highly risky, on which the management discussed and set up certain new processes and stringent controls so that the business can function in an efficient manner. For the financial year ended 31st March 2024, Due Diligence was done for the company, which impacted the company significantly in terms of its reputation and business. The company lost some significant contracts during the process of investigation itself. At the time of due diligence review, the reviewer assessed the business feasibility also so as to assess whether the current business would be more beneficial in future or not. The management of Karma Ltd. did not understand this perspective. The management argued that the reviewer has no powers to assess the business feasibility, as the company was running a profitable business from many years. The company had various litigations going on including those related to matter of taxation. The company had taken consultations in respect of those litigations from professionals and renowned legal/ tax consultants. The reviewer for due diligence reviewed these consultation documents and also asked for the documents related to these matters. Further, he also suggested that the decision taken by the company in some matters was not correct. At the time of investigation, the reviewer asked about the background of the promoters of the company. The management explained that there was no need for this investigation. Further, the management explained that the company has already gone through the processes of due diligence and forensic accounting in the previous years and there was no doubt raised on promoters of the company. So, the background of promoters cannot be shared with the reviewer. Based on the above facts, answer the following MCQs:

questions.question_text: The management argued that the reviewer has no powers to assess the business feasibility, as the company has been running a profitable business from many years. Which of the following statement should be correct?

options.a: The contention of the management was correct.
options.b: Reviewer was correct, as due diligence covers assessment of business feasibility as well.
options.c: Reviewer was correct as due diligence covers assessment of business feasibility as well, however, as the company was doing this business for decades it should not have been carried out by the reviewer.
options.d: Management was correct; however, it should have discussed the same with the investor as part of the sale contract.

questions.explanation_html: Reviewer was correct, as due diligence covers assessment of business feasibility as well. The due diligence process includes “brief description of commercial and/or other activities carried out by the organization” and “the projection of future profitability”, which clearly involves assessment of business feasibility and prospects, irrespective of past profitability.

questions.question_text: The due diligence reviewer was given audited financial statement of the company for his financial review for the year ended March 2024. However, the reviewer asked for financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2023, which was already audited by the statutory auditors of the company and the management of the company declined this request.

options.a: The management is correct.
options.b: Reviewer can ask for documents even for the period for which audit is completed.
options.c: Reviewer can ask for financial statements for the period for which audit is completed but he cannot give any statement on them. He can collect the same for his documentation purpose only as per the requirements of the auditing standards.
options.d: Reviewer has no right to review the financial statements of the period other than the period under review.

questions.explanation_html: Reviewer can ask for documents even for the period for which audit is completed. Due diligence requires review of financial statements and trading results both past and the recent past to evaluate trends and risks. The fact that audit is completed does not restrict the reviewer from reviewing past audited financial statements.

questions.question_text: The reviewer for due diligence reviewed the consultation documents pertaining to various litigations going on including those related to matter of taxation and also asked for the documents related to these matters. Further, he also suggested that the decision taken by the company in some matters was not correct.

options.a: The reviewer needs to have independent assessment of legal/ tax cases and any outcome needs to be discussed with the management.
options.b: The company should not have provided the documents as those are confidential.
options.c: The reviewer can study the tax consultation document but cannot give his opinion as the company already took the opinion from professional consultant.
options.d: Tax and legal matters are not a part of review of due diligence exercise.

questions.explanation_html: The reviewer needs to have independent assessment of legal/ tax cases and any outcome needs to be discussed with the management. Taxation and litigations form an integral component of financial due diligence, and the reviewer is required to look into tax liabilities, pending assessments and litigations to assess financial impact, even if opinions from consultants already exist.

questions.question_text: The management may refuse to share the details of promoters. Comment on this.

options.a: Since the company has already went through due diligence and forensic accounting in the previous years, the management may refuse to provide promoters details to the reviewer.
options.b: As the background of promoters has no bearing on the financials of the company, the reviewer should not ask for the details of promoters and the management may refuse to provide the same.
options.c: Since the company went through processes of forensic accounting in the past, and set up new processes and internal controls, the reviewer should not investigate into the background of promoters.
options.d: The contention of the management is not correct.

questions.explanation_html: The contention of the management is not correct. Financial due diligence specifically requires “brief history of the target company and background of its promoters”. The accountant should begin the financial due diligence review by looking into the history of the company and the background of the promoters, irrespective of earlier due diligence or forensic reviews.

title: CASE SCENARIO 15
passage_html: CA Harman, a practicing Chartered Accountant, intends to fill out the Multi-purpose Empanelment Form (MEF) to be included in the panel for the statutory audit of bank branches for the financial year 2023-24, as hosted by the Professional Development Committee (PDC) of ICAI. The application process requires the submission of XML files of personal income tax returns along with the computation of income. During the relevant financial year for which the information is sought, CA Harman had engaged in currency and commodity derivatives transactions, declaring the resulting income under “Business Income” in his tax return. Additionally, Pitch Private Limited approached CA Harman to digitally sign and upload a resignation form related to Mr. Rohit, one of its directors, on the Registrar of Companies (ROC) portal. However, the signature of Mr. Rohit had been copied and pasted by another director of the company. Without verifying the authenticity of the resignation letter, CA Harman digitally signed the form, which was then uploaded to the ROC portal. Subsequently, CA Harman's actions were brought under scrutiny when the Director (Discipline) of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) received complaints regarding alleged misconduct. Upon investigation, he was found guilty of misconduct, and the competent authority imposed the appropriate penalty in accordance with the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. Based on the above facts, answer the following MCQs:

questions.question_text: Whether CA Harman will be held guilty for reflecting income from currency and commodity derivatives as "Business Income". If yes, under which clause?

options.a: Yes, CA Harman will be held guilty for professional misconduct for reflecting income from currency and commodity derivatives as "Business Income" under Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.
options.b: Yes, CA Harman will be held guilty for professional misconduct for reflecting income from currency and commodity derivatives as "Business Income” under Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.
options.c: No, CA Harman will not be held guilty for professional misconduct for reflecting income from currency and commodity derivatives as "Business Income” under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.
options.d: Yes, CA Harman will be held guilty for professional misconduct for reflecting income from currency and commodity derivatives as "Business Income” under Clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.

questions.explanation_html: Yes, CA Harman will be held guilty for professional misconduct for reflecting income from currency and commodity derivatives as "Business Income" under Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. As per Clause (11) of Part I of First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, a Chartered Accountant in practice will be deemed to be guilty of professional misconduct if he engages in any business or occupation other than the profession of the Chartered Accountant unless permitted by the Council so to engage. Further, in accordance with the announcement of Ethical Standards Board of ICAI, it is not permissible for members in practice to transact in commodity derivative transactions. In such a case, CA Harman would be held guilty of professional misconduct for engaging in business other than profession of Chartered Accountancy.

questions.question_text: Before which authority would CA Harman’s misconduct case be placed for disciplinary proceedings?

options.a: The High Court.
options.b: The Board of Discipline.
options.c: The Disciplinary Committee.
options.d: The Appellate Authority.

questions.explanation_html: The Disciplinary Committee Where the Director (Discipline) is of the opinion that a member is guilty of any professional or other misconduct mentioned in the second schedule or in both the Schedule, he shall place the matter before the Disciplinary Committee.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum punishment that could have been imposed on CA Harman under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949?

options.a: Reprimand the member.
options.b: Removal of name from the register of members permanently or for a specified period and fine up to ₹ 5,00,000.
options.c: Suspension of practice for up to 3 months.
options.d: Warning and fine up to ₹ 50,000.

questions.explanation_html: Reprimand the member. CA Harman was found guilty of professional misconduct under Clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule and Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. The matter would have been placed before Disciplinary Committee as it’s allied to both the Schedule because as per the Chartered Accountant Act, 1949 if the matter is allied to the Second Schedule or Both it is referred to the Disciplinary Committee. The minimum punishment that the Disciplinary Committee could have imposed would be: (I) Reprimand the member (II) Remove the name of the member from the Register permanently or for such period as it may think fit. (III) Impose such a fine which may extend to rupees five lakhs.

title: CASE SCENARIO 16
passage_html:
Chartered Accountant Firms - Tink & Co., Llyods & Co. and Manohar & Co. respectively, were appointed as the joint auditors for conducting the statutory audit for the financial year 2023-24 of Anitya Ltd. They were having difference of opinion with regards to the following points:-
S No. Reasons for Differences in Opinion
1 Manohar & Co. wanted to refer to the work of the auditor’s expert, Mr.
Tanmay in the audit report but the other joint auditors were not
agreeing on the same as such reference was not relevant to an
understanding in the final audit opinion and also it was not required
by any statute.
2 Certain misstatements affected information to be included in
‘Management Discussion and Analysis’ of Anitya Ltd.’s annual report
but as they were lower than materiality set for the financial statements
as a whole and so according to the Llyods & Co., there was no
requirement to perform any audit procedures on the same but the
other joint auditors were not agreeing on the same for the reason that
the information may reasonably be expected to influence the
economic decisions of the users of the financial statements.
3 For a selected item, the joint auditors were not able to apply the
designed audit procedures or suitable alternate procedures and Llyods
& Co. wanted to treat that item as a misstatement in the case of test
of controls as well as in the case of test of details but the other joint
auditors were not agreeing on the said treatment.
4 Manohar & Co. had determined for a particular account balance
positive confirmation request was necessary to obtain sufficient and
appropriate audit evidence but as it had not obtained such
confirmation and alternate audit evidence would not have sufficed its
requirements, Manohar & Co. wanted to determine its implications on
the audit opinion but the other joint auditors were not agreeing on
the same.
The differences in opinion in the case of Tink & Co. and Llyods & Co. were resolved but there remained disagreement with the one of the opinions of Manohar & Co. due to which Manohar & Co. expressed its opinion in a separate audit report. Further, Manohar & Co. resigned and filed the required statement with respect to its resignation with Anitya Ltd. as well as the Registrar, respectively. The Board of Directors of Anitya Ltd. appointed Namo & Co. as a joint auditor in place of Manohar & Co. which was later approved by members in the general meeting of the company. Namo & Co. before getting appointed, as aforesaid, had :- (i) Communicated vide a registered post acknowledgment due to the previous joint auditor, Manohar & Co. but the said post was received back with the remarks “Office Found Locked”. (ii) Ascertained that the requirements of Section 139 and Section 140 of the Companies Act, 2013, with the respect to its appointment had been duly complied with or not by Anitya Ltd. Based on the above facts, answer the following:

questions.question_text: Whether the opinion of Manohar & Co. for referring the work of the auditor’s expert, Mr. Tanmay in the audit report, can be considered as valid?

options.a: No, as such reference was not relevant to an understanding in the final audit opinion and also it was not required by any law or regulation.
options.b: Yes, such a reference in the auditor’s opinion was relevant to the understanding of the users of the financial statement.
options.c: No, as such reference was not required by any law or regulation.
options.d: Yes, if such reference was relevant to any ‘key audit matter’ as per SA 701 even though it was not required by any law or regulation.

questions.explanation_html: No, as such reference was not relevant to an understanding in the final audit opinion and also it was not required by any law or regulation. As per SA 620 “Using the Work of an Auditor’s Expert”, the auditor shall not refer to the work of an auditor’s expert in an auditor’s report containing an unmodified opinion unless required by law or regulation to do so. If such reference is required by law or regulation, the auditor shall indicate in the auditor’s report that the reference does not reduce the auditor’s responsibility for the audit opinion.

questions.question_text: Whether the opinion of Llyods & Co. for treating the item as a misstatement in the case of test of controls as well in the case of test of details for which the joint auditors were not able to apply the designed audit procedures or suitable alternate procedures, can be considered as valid?

options.a: No, as such item shall be as a misstatement only in the case of test of controls and for test of details such item shall be treated as a deviation.
options.b: Yes, as such item shall be treated as a misstatement in the case of test of controls and test of details.
options.c: No, as such item shall be treated as a deviation in the case of test of controls and test of details.
options.d: No, as such item shall be treated as a misstatement only in the case of test of details and for test of controls such item shall be treated as a deviation.

questions.explanation_html: No, as such item shall be treated as a misstatement only in the case of test of details and for test of controls such item shall be treated as a deviation. As per SA 530 “Audit Sampling”, if the auditor is unable to apply the designed audit procedures, or suitable alternative procedures, to a selected item, the auditor shall treat that item as a deviation from the prescribed control, in the case of tests of controls, or a misstatement, in the case of tests of details.

questions.question_text: Whether the insistence by Manohar & Co. for determining implications of not obtaining response to positive confirmation request on the audit opinion can be considered as valid?

options.a: No, because in such a case the auditor should have enquired the reasons for the same from the management in writing and included the same as a ‘Key Audit Matter’ as per SA 701
options.b: Yes, because in such a case the auditor should have determined implications for the audit and the auditor’s opinion in accordance with SA 705.
options.c: No, because in such a case the auditor should have obtained and relied upon a written representation as per SA 580 in this regard.
options.d: No, because in such a case the auditor should have determined the need to include an ‘Emphasis of matter’ paragraph in the audit report as per SA 706 after considering the implications on the audit.

questions.explanation_html: Yes, because in such a case the auditor should have determined implications for the audit and the auditor’s opinion in accordance with SA 705. As per SA 505 “External Confirmations”, if the auditor has determined that a response to a positive confirmation request is necessary to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, alternative audit procedures will not provide the audit evidence the auditor requires. If the auditor does not obtain such confirmation, the auditor shall determine the implications for the audit and the auditor’s opinion in accordance with SA 705.

questions.question_text: Whether Namo & Co. would be considered to have satisfied the requirements of communicating with the previous auditor?

options.a: No, as the communication through registered post acknowledgment due could not be done, Namo & Co. should have tried an alternative form of communication as prescribed by the Council of the ICAI for the same.
options.b: Yes, as it would be deemed that such post was delivered.
options.c: No, because in such a case Namo & Co. should have informed the Council of the ICAI with respect to the non-delivery of post to the previous auditor along with the reasons for the same.
options.d: No, however, Namo & Co. can commence the audit of Anitya Ltd. but should try to satisfy the requirement of communicating with the previous auditor at least before signing of the audit report.

questions.explanation_html: Yes, as it would be deemed that such post was delivered. The communication received back by the Incoming Auditor with “Office found Locked” written on the Acknowledgement Due shall be deemed as having been delivered to the retiring auditor. Thus, it would be considered to have satisfied the requirements of communicating with the previous auditor.

title: CASE SCENARIO 17
passage_html: CA Kamlesh was appointed as the engagement partner on behalf of Dutta & Associates for conducting the statutory audit for 3rd consecutive year of Pramat Limited, an unlisted public company, with a turnover of ₹ 35 crore during F.Y. 2022-23. From F.Y. 2023-24 onwards, Pramat Limited had voluntarily adopted to prepare its financial statements as per Division II of Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, due to which Dutta & Associates had revised the terms of audit engagement for the current audit engagement. As per the revised terms, it was decided that the auditor’s report on the financial statements will incorporate a paragraph in accordance with SA 706, drawing users’ attention to the additional disclosures. Moreover, it was decided that management will also present appropriate disclosures in the financial statements with respect to this change. While auditing the entity, CA Kamlesh came across a business policy of Pramat Limited that required to invest some portion of its money earned in its business in securities of different blue-chip companies and due to this reason, almost 55% of Pramat Limited’s total assets consisted of such investments. These securities transactions were handled by its broker company, River Securities Private Limited (RSPL). RSPL was also performing necessary investment account reconciliations and was also preparing the MTM gain and loss calculation for the entity. Pramat Limited used to rely upon the calculations performed by RSPL and based on that they pass the MTM entry for their current investments every month. Pramat Limited relying on the controls presents in RSPL for the preparation of this entry. They also listed controls present in RSPL in their Risk Control Matrix as key controls. The engagement quality reviewer, CA Tushar, recommended CA Kamlesh to obtain a Type 2 report from the management of RSPL to which CA Kamlesh said that it was not required to do so as management was already comfortable with the controls present in RSPL. While finalising the audit report, CA Kamlesh prepared a letter containing key important points to be communicated to Those Charged with the Governance and Audit Committee of the entity. This letter was prepared in addition to the audit report. The audit team was of the view that for the above-mentioned letter the audit team is required to generate UDIN. Based on the above facts, answer the following:

questions.question_text: While finalising the audit report CA Kamlesh decided to present the early adoption of IND AS under the “Other Matter Paragraph” as in the auditor’s judgment, is relevant to users’ understanding of the audit, the auditor’s responsibilities or the auditor’s report. Kindly guide CA Kamlesh with respect to correct reporting in the Audit Report as per SA 706:

options.a: No disclosure is required as it is voluntary adoption of Division II of Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013.
options.b: The Audit team should report the change in the “Emphasis of Matter Paragraph” because, in the auditor’s judgment, it is of such importance that it is fundamental to users’ understanding of the financial statements.
options.c: The Audit team should report the change in the “Other Matter Paragraph” because, in the auditor’s judgment, it is of such importance that it is fundamental to users’ understanding of the financial statements.
options.d: The Audit team should qualify as per SA 705 the said change as it was not required to be implemented and this will create unnecessary confusion for the read.

questions.explanation_html: The Audit team should report the change in the “Emphasis of Matter Paragraph” because, in the auditor’s judgment, it is of such importance that it is fundamental to users’ understanding of the financial statements. As per SA 706 “Emphasis of Matter Paragraphs and Other Matter Paragraphs in the Independent Auditor’s Report”, early application (where permitted) of a new accounting standard that has a material effect on the financial statements is one of the circumstance where the auditor may consider it necessary to include an Emphasis of Matter paragraph.

questions.question_text: CA Kamlesh ’s risk assessment includes an expectation that controls at the service organization are operating effectively and he contended that there was no requirement to obtain a Type 2 report. Kindly guide CA Kamlesh with respect to the requirement of SA 402.

options.a: CA Kamlesh ’s contention is correct as Management has comfort over the controls at service organization for the transactions and activities which are processed there.
options.b: When the user auditor’s risk assessment includes an expectation that controls at the service organization are operating effectively, the user auditor shall obtain audit evidence about the operating effectiveness of those controls which may include by obtaining Type 2 report.
options.c: It depends upon the auditor’s judgment and the recommendation of the engagement quality reviewer is not binding upon Audit team. As a result, CA Kamlesh’s decision will be considered correct and appropriate.
options.d: As no services are outsourced to the broker company and hence there is no need to obtain the type 2 report.

questions.explanation_html:
When the user auditor’s risk assessment includes an expectation that controls at the service organization are operating effectively, the user auditor shall obtain audit evidence about the operating effectiveness of those controls which may include by obtaining Type 2 report. As per SA 402 “Audit Considerations Relating to an Entity Using a Service Organisation”, when the user auditor’s risk assessment includes an expectation that controls at the service organisation are operating effectively, the user auditor shall obtain audit evidence about the operating effectiveness of those controls from one or more of the following procedures:

(i) Obtaining a Type 2 report, if available;

(ii) Performing appropriate tests of controls at the service organisation; or

(iii) Using another auditor to perform tests of controls at the service organisation on behalf of the user auditor.

questions.question_text: CA Kamlesh was not sure with respect to the UDIN requirement for the letter to Those Charged with Governance containing important audit topics and findings for discussion. Kindly guide CA Kamlesh with respect to UDIN requirements for this letter.

options.a: Separate UDINs are to be generated for the Statutory audit report and Letter to Those Charged with Governance.
options.b: UDIN is only required for the Statutory Audit Report, but it is not required for the communication performed by Auditor as per SA 260 and SA 265.
options.c: One single UDIN is required to be generated for all items for this Client. UDINs are required to be generated Client wise instead of report-wise.
options.d: One single UDIN will be generated for the whole year for this engagement which may include various communication by auditor to management and Those Charged with Governance.

questions.explanation_html: UDIN is only required for the Statutory Audit Report, but it is not required for the communication performed by Auditor as per SA 260 and SA 265. UDIN is mandatory from 1st July, 2019 on all Corporate/ Non- Corporate Audit, Attest and Assurance Functions. Thus, a member of the Institute in practice shall generate Unique Document Identification Number (UDIN) for all kinds of the certification, GST and Tax Audit Reports and other Audit, Assurance and Attestation functions undertaken/signed by him. Communications with Those Charged with Governance under SA 260 and SA 265 do not require UDIN, as these are not audit reports or certificates.

title: CASE SCENARIO 19
passage_html:
Innovate Robotics Pvt. Ltd. (IRPL) engaged in the business of manufacturing advanced robotic machinery and developing proprietary automation software appointed M/s Gaur & Associates, Chartered Accountants, as the statutory auditor for the financial year 2024-25. The financial highlights of IRPL for the year were as follows:
Particulars Balance as at
31st March 2024)
Total Turnover (Previous Year: ₹ 85 crores) ₹ 120 crores
Borrowings from banks and financial institutions ₹ 35 crores
Paid-up Share Capital ₹ 20 crores
Profit Before Tax ₹ 15 crores
During the audit, Engagement Partner CA. Gaurav and his team observed the various issues which are given as under: (i) While conducting substantive procedures, the audit team noticed a significant increase in sales during the last quarter of the financial year. A major portion of this increase, amounting to ₹ 8 crores, was attributed to sales made to a new customer, TechSynergy Solutions Pvt. Ltd., which was incorporated on 1st October, 2024. The audit team’s inquiries revealed that the payment for these sales was received on 5th April, 2025, just before the audit commenced. Upon further investigation, Anjali, an audit assistant, discovered that one of the directors of TechSynergy Solutions was the husband of the daughter of IRPL's Chief Financial Officer (CFO), Mr. Alok. When CA. Gaurav brought this information to Mr. Alok’s attention, the CFO dismissed it as a mere coincidence and insisted that the transaction was conducted at arm’s length. He also argued that since the payment was fully received, there was no risk of a misstatement. Management also refused to disclose this relationship in the financial statements, contending that it was not a related party transaction as per the applicable financial reporting framework, and that doing so would unnecessarily complicate matters. It was also observed that approval by way of resolution was also not obtained by management before entering into the contract with TechSynergy for sale of goods. (ii) During the physical verification of Property, Plant, and Equipment (PPE), the audit team & management could not locate a highly specialised robotic arm, which was recorded in the fixed asset register with a written down value of ₹ 2.5 crores. Later, management provided a verbal explanation that the asset had been sent to a facility in Germany for immediate calibration in February 2025 and was in transit. However, they failed to provide any supporting documentation such as gate pass, dispatch challan, or insurance documentation for this movement. This matter remained unresolved at the time of finalisation of the audit report. (iii) IRPL holds 60% equity shares in a subsidiary, AutoBots Ltd. The statutory auditors of AutoBots Ltd., in their audit report for FY 2024–25, expressed a qualified opinion due to non-provision of doubtful debts amounting to ₹ 1.5 crores, which the auditor considered materially misstated. During the final phase of the audit, on 15th April 2025, IRPL's CEO offered a position of 'Head of Software Development' to CA. Gaurav's wife, a highly qualified software engineer. CA. Gaurav subsequently discovered that his father purchased 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹ 10 each in AutoBots Ltd., a subsidiary of IRPL on 27th June, 2025 i.e., after issuance of audit report. The total paid-up capital of AutoBots Ltd. is ₹ 5 crores. In the final meeting on 25th April 2025, IRPL's management strongly contended that the unresolved matters were minor in the context of their overall profitable operations. They urged CA. Gaurav to issue an unmodified audit opinion, warning that any modification could jeopardize a crucial funding deal for the company. Based on the above facts, answer the following:

questions.question_text: With reference to the ₹ 8 crore sales transaction with TechSynergy Solutions Pvt. Ltd., and management’s refusal to disclose the relationship with the entity, how should CA. Gaurav assess this matter in accordance with SA 240?

options.a: CA. Gaurav should accept the CFO’s explanation and conclude that the transaction does not pose a significant risk, as the payment was fully received subsequent to the year-end, which mitigates the risk of financial loss.
options.b: CA. Gaurav should treat the transaction as indicative of a significant risk of material misstatement and consider the implications for the audit, including the reliability of management's representations, regardless of the subsequent payment.
options.c: CA. Gaurav can rely on the management's assertion that the transaction was at arm's length and that the relationship does not meet the technical definition of a related party, thereby concluding that no further action is necessary.
options.d: CA. Gaurav should only request a written representation from management confirming the nature of the transaction and their assertion that no related party relationship exists and then proceed to issue an unmodified opinion.

questions.explanation_html: CA. Gaurav should treat the transaction as indicative of a significant risk of material misstatement and consider the implications for the audit, including the reliability of management's representations, regardless of the subsequent payment. SA 240, "The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud in an Audit of Financial Statements," requires the auditor to maintain professional skepticism and investigate significant unusual transactions. The sale to TechSynergy Solutions, a newly incorporated entity, in the last quarter, which significantly inflates revenue without necessary and requisite approvals under Section 188 of the Companies Act, is a red flag. The discovery that a director of TechSynergy is related to the CFO, combined with management's refusal to disclose this, strongly indicates a risk of fraudulent financial reporting (e.g., to overstate revenue).

questions.question_text: What is the reporting responsibility of CA. Gaurav under para 3(i) of CARO 2020, regarding the undisposed robotic arm with a written down value of ₹ 2.5 crores that was not physically located?

options.a: Since the management has provided a verbal explanation that the asset is in transit for calibration, CA. Gaurav should accept it and is not required to report any discrepancy in the CARO report.
options.b: The discrepancy is not considered material as it represents only a small portion of the company's total turnover of ₹ 120 crores, and therefore, no reporting under CARO 2020 is necessary.
options.c: CA. Gaurav should state in his CARO report that a material discrepancy of ₹ 2.5 crores was noticed during the physical verification of Property, Plant, and Equipment, and this has not been properly dealt with in the books of account.
options.d:
CA. Gaurav should qualify his main audit report for this matter but can choose not to mention this specific discrepancy in the CARO report to avoid redundancy.

of ₹ 10 lakhs in AutoBots Ltd., the subsidiary company, on 1st April, 2025,
what is the implication on the audit engagement of IRPL under the
Companies Act, 2013 and the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949?

(c) Since CA. Gaurav was not aware of his father's investment at the time of accepting the audit, he is not in violation, provided he now obtains
a declaration from his father confirming it is not a material investment.

4. What is the most appropriate type of audit opinion that CA. Gaurav should express for IRPL's financial statements in accordance with SA 700
regarding multiple unresolved issues, specifically the ₹ 8 crore revenue
transaction, the missing ₹ 2.5 crore asset and the impact of the
subsidiary's qualified opinion?

(b) A qualified opinion, as the issues identified are material but are confined to specific elements of the financial statements and are not
pervasive.
high-risk areas.
5. If CA. Gaurav surrenders to the pressure from IRPL's management and issues an unmodified audit report for the year ended 31st March 2025,
despite the unresolved issues regarding the revenue transaction with
TechSynergy and the unverified robotic arm, he would be guilty of
professional misconduct. Which of the following clauses of Part I of the
Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, would be
applicable?
applicable? (a) Clause 5 and 9 (b) Clause 6 and 4 (c) Clause 5 and 8 (d) Clause 5, 6 and 7

questions.explanation_html:
CA. Gaurav should state in his CARO report that a material discrepancy of ₹ 2.5 crores was noticed during the physical verification of Property, Plant, and Equipment, and this has not been properly dealt with in the books of account. Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020, requires the auditor to state whether any material discrepancies were noticed on physical verification of Property, Plant, and Equipment and if so, whether they have been properly dealt with in the books of account. A fixed asset with a WDV of ₹ 2.5 crores being physically untraceable without any supporting documentation (like a gate pass, challan, or insurance) constitutes a material discrepancy. Management's verbal explanation is insufficient audit evidence. Therefore, CA Gaurav must report this material discrepancy and the fact that it has not been properly accounted for.
because his relative holds securities in a subsidiary of the company
exceeding the prescribed limit of ₹ 1 lakh, and continuing the
engagement constitutes professional misconduct.		 CA. Gaurav is disqualified from being the auditor of IRPL
statements as a whole are misleading. An adverse opinion is appropriate in this scenario. According to SA 705 (Revised), an auditor should express an adverse opinion when, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, they conclude that misstatements, individually or in the aggregate, are both material and pervasive to the financial statements. The situation involves: 1. A potential fraudulent revenue transaction of ₹8 crores, where management refuses disclosure, casting doubt on their integrity. This misstatement alone is highly material relative to the Profit Before Tax of ₹15 crores. 2. An unverified asset of ₹2.5 crores with no supporting documentation. 3. The effect of a qualified opinion in a subsidiary. The combination of these issues, particularly the one related to revenue which suggests management override and potential fraud, is not isolated. It indicates a pervasive lack of reliability in the financial statements. Therefore, the financial statements as a whole are materially misstated and misleading.

title: CASE SCENARIO 20
passage_html: SCL is a prominent, listed Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) (non-deposit taking NBFCs with an asset size of ₹ 1,000 crore and above) primarily engaged in providing corporate loans and retail financing. Mehta & Shah Associates (MSA), a partnership firm with two partners, CA. Karan Mehta and CA. Arjun Shah, was appointed as the statutory auditor of SwiftFin Capital Ltd. (SCL) for the financial year ended 31st March, 2025. During the audit, MSA team led by CA. Mehta, began reviewing SCL's compliance with RBI's Master Directions for NBFCs. They discovered that three large corporate loan accounts, with a total outstanding balance of ₹ 15 crores, had principal and/or interest payments overdue for a period ranging from 95 to 110 days as at the balance sheet date. However, these accounts were still classified as 'Standard Assets' in the company's records. The management of SCL argued that these were long-standing, "blue-chip" clients with whom they were in advanced restructuring negotiations. They contended that classifying these accounts as Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) would trigger cross-default clauses in other agreements of those clients and permanently damage valuable business relationships. They insisted that the non-classification was a temporary measure based on commercial judgment. While reviewing the board minutes, the audit team came to know about a lawsuit filed against SCL in January 2025. A group of retail customers alleged that the company had provided loans by charging interest rates that were not transparently disclosed and were in violation of the RBI's Fair Practices Code. SCL's internal legal department had prepared a note for the board estimating a financial outcome of up to ₹ 5 crores if the judgment went against the company. However, the financial statements contained no provision or disclosure for this matter. Management asserted that their legal advisors believed the probability of an unfavourable outcome was "remote". In April 2025, impressed with the firm's diligence, the management of SCL also offered the tax audit engagement under Section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961, to MSA for the Assessment Year 2025-26. CA. Mehta reviewed the firm's workload for the assessment year. As on that date, CA. Mehta had already signed 55 tax audit reports, and his partner, CA. Arjun, had signed 60 tax audit reports. Based on the above facts, answer the following:

questions.question_text: Considering the requirements of SA 250, "Consideration of Laws and Regulations in an Audit of Financial Statements" and the specific context of an NBFC audit, what is the most appropriate course of action for CA. Mehta regarding the non-classification of loan accounts worth ₹ 15 crores as NPAs?

options.a: CA. Mehta should accept management's commercial judgment, as advanced restructuring negotiations are in progress, and disclose the matter in an "Emphasis of Matter" paragraph to ensure user awareness.
options.b: CA. Mehta should inform the management that this non-classification constitutes a material misstatement due to non-compliance with RBI's mandatory prudential norms. If management refuses to correct this by reclassifying the assets and making provisions, he must modify the audit opinion.
options.c: CA. Mehta's primary responsibility is to report this specific instance of non-compliance with IRAC norms to the Department of Supervision of the RBI, and he can issue an unmodified opinion on the financial statements.
options.d: CA. Mehta should obtain a specific written representation from management confirming the future recoverability of the loans and based on this representation, he can agree to the existing classification and issue a clean report.

questions.explanation_html: CA. Mehta should inform the management that this non- classification constitutes a material misstatement due to non-compliance with RBI's mandatory prudential norms. If management refuses to correct this by reclassifying the assets and making provisions, he must modify the audit opinion. The RBI's Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification, and Provisioning (IRAC norms) are laws and regulations that have a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures in an NBFC's financial statements. According to SA 250 “Consideration of Laws and Regulations in an Audit of Financial Statements”, the auditor has a responsibility to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding compliance with such laws and regulations. The overdue status of over 90 days requires a mandatory classification as NPA. Management's "commercial judgment" cannot override these specific regulatory requirements. This non-classification results in a material misstatement of assets and profits. Therefore, CA Mehta must request management to correct the financials. If they refuse, he is obligated under SA 705 (Revised) to issue a modified opinion (qualified or adverse, depending on pervasiveness).

questions.question_text: With reference to the tax audit engagement offered by SCL and assuming that the CA. Arjun is finalised as the signing on behalf of the firm Mehta & Shah Associates (MSA), can the firm legally accept this new Tax Audit assignment for the Assessment Year 2025-26 as per the guidelines issued by the Council of ICAI?

options.a: No, the firm cannot accept the engagement because the total number of tax audits conducted by the partner CA. Arjun (60) is very close to the limit, and accepting one more would be a violation.
options.b: Yes, the firm can accept the engagement, but the audit report must be signed by CA. Mehta, as CA. Arjun has already reached his permissible limit of 60 audits.
options.c: No, the firm cannot accept the engagement because the specified limit of 60 tax audits applies to the firm as a whole, and the partners' individual counts are irrelevant.
options.d: Yes, the firm can accept the engagement because the specified limit of 60 tax audits applies to each partner individually, and the firm can still take five more Tax Audits before reaching its 120 Tax Audit limit.

questions.explanation_html: Yes, the firm can accept the engagement because the specified limit of 60 tax audits applies to each partner individually, and the firm can still take five more Tax Audits before reaching its 120 Tax Audit limit. According to the Council General Guidelines, 2008 (Chapter VI), a Chartered Accountant in practice is permitted to conduct a maximum of 60 tax audits under Section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961, per assessment year. This limit is applicable per partner in a firm. Paragraph 6.1.7 of Chapter VI of Council General Guidelines, 2008, clarifies that the limit on the number of tax audit assignments per partner in a CA Firm may be distributed between the partners in any manner whatsoever. In the case of MSA, which has two partners, the firm can collectively handle up to 120 tax audits (60 for CA Mehta + 60 for CA Shah). As of the offer date, CA Mehta has signed 55 and CA Shah has signed 60 reports. Therefore, the firm can legally accept the new tax audit, and it can be signed by either of the partners.

questions.question_text: CA. Mehta has identified the matter regarding NPA classification and the non-disclosure of the lawsuit as the two most significant issues of the entire audit. He wishes to highlight these matters prominently in his report as Key Audit Matters. Considering the nature of matters, which of the following is the only appropriate method for CA. Mehta to communicate these in his audit report?

options.a: Describe both issues in detail in the "Key Audit Matters" (KAM) section, as they represent the areas of highest risk and significant auditor judgment.
options.b: Describe both issues in an "Emphasis of Matter" (EOM) paragraph, as they are fundamental to understanding the company's financial position and risks.
options.c: Describe the issues giving rise to the misstatements in the "Basis for Modification" paragraph, which will support a qualified or adverse opinion.
options.d: Describe the issues in an "Other Matter" (OM) paragraph, as they are relevant to the users' understanding of the conduct of the audit and management's integrity.

questions.explanation_html: Describe the issues giving rise to the misstatements in the "Basis for Modification" paragraph, which will support a qualified or adverse opinion. Since there are identified material misstatements that management has refused to correct, this is the only appropriate placement for these matters.

questions.question_text: Apart from making inquiries with management wherein the management’s assessment of the lawsuit is "remote," which audit procedures should be designed and performed by CA. Mehta?

options.a: He should discuss the matter with audit committee, expressing concern that management's representation is unreliable and insists on making a provision of ₹ 5 crores required in the financial statements based on the available evidence and his independent assessment.
options.b: He should seek direct communication with the entity’s external legal counsel through a letter of inquiry, prepared and sent by management, requesting the entity’s external legal counsel to provide a necessary update on the litigation.
options.c: He should seek direct communication with the entity’s external legal counsel through a letter of inquiry, prepared by management and sent by the auditor, requesting the entity’s external legal counsel to communicate directly with the auditor.
options.d: After seeking direct communication with the entity’s external legal, he should independently engage a forensic accountant at the firm's own cost to obtain the evidence against the lawsuit, which should be admissible in the court of law.

questions.explanation_html: He should seek direct communication with the entity’s external legal counsel through a letter of inquiry, prepared by management and sent by the auditor, requesting the entity’s external legal counsel to communicate directly with the auditor. If the auditor assesses a risk of material misstatement regarding litigation or claims that have been identified, or when audit procedures performed indicate that other material litigation or claims may exist, the auditor shall, in addition to the procedures required by other SAs, seek direct communication with the entity’s external legal counsel. The auditor shall do so through a letter of inquiry, prepared by management and sent by the auditor, requesting the entity’s external legal counsel to communicate directly with the auditor.

title: CASE SCENARIO 21
passage_html: Prakriti Limited is a listed company engaged in the manufacture of eco-friendly home appliances. During the financial year, the company significantly expanded its operations by setting up a new manufacturing facility in a semi-rural location. The expansion was aimed at increasing production capacity while benefiting from lower operational costs and proximity to raw material suppliers. During the statutory audit of Prakriti Limited, the auditor became aware of the undisclosed environmental violations and labour-related non-compliances. Management represented that the issues were operational in nature and assured corrective action. Relying on management representations, the auditor did not include any specific reference to these matters in the audit report. The company sources raw materials from a diverse supplier base and employs a large workforce, a substantial portion of which consists of contractual labour engaged through third-party contractors. Prakriti Limited sells its products through online platforms as well as a widespread network of distributors across India. Being a listed entity, Prakriti Limited is required to comply with the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework. During the year, the following issues came to the attention of stakeholders and regulators: • Prakriti Limited has published its sustainability policies and environmental commitments on its official website. However, certain material environmental violations relating to emissions and waste management at the newly established plant were disclosed to the public only after these violations were highlighted in media reports. The company did not make timely or voluntary disclosures to its stakeholders when the violations first occurred. • Contractual workers employed at the new manufacturing facility raised complaints regarding delayed payment of wages by contractors and absence of adequate safety measures at the workplace. The workers alleged that despite being aware of these issues, the company did not take sufficient steps to ensure compliance by contractors. • Prakriti Limited collects customer data through its online sales platform for order processing and customer engagement. During the year, it was observed that the company shared customer data with third-party marketing agencies without obtaining explicit consent from customers. Statutory auditor CA. Manik, during the statutory audit of Prakriti Limited, became aware of the undisclosed environmental violations and labour-related non-compliances. Management represented that the issues were operational in nature and assured corrective action. Relying on management representations, the auditor did not include any specific reference to these matters in the audit report. Based on the above facts, answer the following:

questions.question_text: The delayed disclosure of environmental violations at the new manufacturing plant is contrary to which BRSR principle?

options.a: Principle 2 – Safe and Sustainable Goods and Services
options.b: Principle 1 – Ethics, Transparency and Accountability
options.c: Principle 6 – Protection and Restoration of Environment
options.d: Principle 9 – Provide Value to the Consumers in a Responsible Manner

questions.explanation_html: Principle 1 – Ethics, Transparency and Accountability Principle 1 requires businesses to conduct operations with integrity and transparency and to ensure timely, accurate and complete disclosure of material information to stakeholders. Delayed disclosure of environmental violations, especially after media intervention, reflects a lack of transparency and accountability, thereby violating Principle 1.

questions.question_text: Which clause of CARO, 2020 is most likely to require reporting in respect of delayed wages and labour-related statutory non-compliances at Prakriti Limited?

options.a: Clause 3(vii) – Statutory Dues
options.b: Clause 3(i) – Property, Plant and Equipment;
options.c: Clause 3(xi) – Fraud by the company
options.d: Clause 3(xv) – Non-cash transactions with directors

questions.explanation_html: Clause 3(vii) – undisputed statutory dues Clause (vii) of Paragraph 3 of CARO, 2020 requires reporting on whether the company is regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues including Goods and Services Tax, provident fund, employees' state insurance, income-tax, sales-tax, service tax, duty of customs, duty of excise, value added tax, cess and any other statutory dues to the appropriate authorities and if not, the extent of the arrears of outstanding statutory dues as on the last day of the financial year concerned for a period of more than six months from the date they became payable, shall be indicated.

questions.question_text: The grievances raised by contractual workers regarding delayed wages and unsafe working conditions primarily indicate non-compliance with which principle?

options.a: Principle 4 – Respect for Stakeholders’ Interests and Responsiveness
options.b: Principle 2 – Safe and Sustainable Goods and Services
options.c: Principle 8 – Promote Inclusive Growth and Equitable Development
options.d: Principle 3 – Promote Well-Being of All Employees Including those in the Value Chain

questions.explanation_html: Principle 3 – Promote Well-Being of All Employees Including Those in the Value Chain Principle 3 extends beyond permanent employees and includes workers in the value chain, such as contractual labour. Timely payment of wages and provision of safe working conditions are core elements of employee well-being. Failure to address wage delays and workplace safety concerns indicates non-compliance with this principle.

questions.question_text: Which is the most appropriate response of the auditor upon becoming aware of environmental and labour law non-compliances as per relevant Standards on Auditing?

options.a: Accept management representation as sufficient audit evidence
options.b: Ignore the matters since they relate to non-financial reporting
options.c: Evaluate implications under applicable laws and communicate with those charged with governance, and consider appropriate reporting
options.d: Immediately resign from the audit

questions.explanation_html: Evaluate implications under applicable laws and communicate with those charged with governance, and consider appropriate reporting As per SA 250, the auditor must consider non-compliance with laws and regulations and communicate with those charged with governance. Further, reliance solely on management representation by the auditor violates SA 580 and the principle of professional skepticism.

questions.question_text: Sharing customer data with third-party marketing agencies without explicit consent amounts to a violation of:

options.a: Principle 2 – Safe and Sustainable Goods and Services:
options.b: Principle 4 – Respect for Stakeholders’ Interests and Responsiveness
options.c: Principle 5 – Respect and Promote Human Rights
options.d: Principle 9 – Provide Value to the Consumers in a Responsible Manner

questions.explanation_html: Principle 9 – Provide Value to the Consumers in a Responsible Manner Principle 9 emphasises responsible engagement with customers, including protection of customer data and privacy. Sharing personal data with third parties without explicit consent infringes upon customers’ right to privacy and violates the responsible business conduct expected under this principle.

title: CASE SCENARIO 22
passage_html: Wire Ltd. is a listed company engaged in the manufacture of electrical equipment. The company operates multiple manufacturing units across India and consumes significant quantities of electricity, water, and natural resources such as copper and aluminium for its operations. The production process results in carbon emissions, water discharge, hazardous waste, and e-waste. To address environmental concerns, Wire Ltd. has installed solar power facilities at its plants and implemented water recycling systems. The company has also set measurable targets to reduce its carbon emissions by 30% over the next five years and periodically tracks its emission levels. Wire Ltd. employs a large workforce, including permanent and contract workers. The company has framed policies relating to employee health and safety, labour welfare, gender diversity, equal opportunity, and skill development. It also undertakes community development initiatives in the areas surrounding its manufacturing units. The Board of Wire Ltd. comprises executive and independent directors. The company has constituted various Board committees, including the Audit Committee, Nomination and Remuneration Committee, and Risk Management Committee. Wire Ltd. follows a code of conduct, has a whistle-blower mechanism, and ensures compliance with applicable laws and regulations. In response to increasing investor and regulatory expectations, Wire Ltd. has initiated Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) reporting, which includes both qualitative disclosures (such as policies and strategies) and quantitative disclosures (such as metrics and key performance indicators). Wire Ltd. appoints a firm of Chartered Accountants APR & Associates to provide ESG assurance using advanced digital auditing tools such as data analytics and automated extraction of ESG data from its ERP systems. Subsequently, CA. Ankur, Partner APR & Associates instruct his article assistant CA Mihir to publish a detailed post on its website and social media platforms highlighting its role in conducting “ESG and Digital Audits of a listed manufacturing company using AI-based tools” and to invites other corporates to approach the firm for similar assignments. Based on the above facts, answer the following:

questions.question_text: Which of the following activities undertaken by Wire Ltd. falls under the Environmental (E) pillar of ESG?

options.a: Constitution of Board-level committees
options.b: Adoption of a whistle-blower mechanism
options.c: Installation of solar power facilities and water recycling systems
options.d: Community development initiatives

questions.explanation_html: Installation of solar power facilities and water recycling systems The environmental pillar include the following elements as under: • Climate Change: Carbon Emissions, Product Carbon FootPrints, Financing Environmental Impact, Climate Change Vulnerability • Natural Resources: Water Stress, Bio-diversity & land use, Raw Material sourcing • Pollution & Waste: Toxic emission and waste, Packing Material and waste, E- Waste • Environment Opportunity: Clean Tech, Green Building, Renewable Energy

questions.question_text: Policies relating to labour welfare, gender diversity, and community development primarily relate to which pillar of ESG?

options.a: Environmental Pillar
options.b: Social Pillar
options.c: Governance Pillar
options.d: Financial Pillar

questions.explanation_html: Social The Social pillars include the following elements as under: • Labour Management • Health & Safety • Human Capital Development • Supply Chain Labour Standards

questions.question_text: Whether the instruction of CA Ankur, Partner of APR & Associates, to his articled assistant CA Mihir is in compliance with the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and the Schedules thereto?

options.a: Yes, since publication of information relating to professional expertise and use of digital audit tools is permitted under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and the Schedules thereto.
options.b: No, as the instruction results in indirect solicitation of professional work, thereby violating Clause 6 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.
options.c: No, as the instruction results in indirect solicitation of professional work, thereby violating Clause 6 of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.
options.d: Yes, since ESG assurance and digital auditing are emerging areas and are not restricted provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and the Schedules thereto.

questions.explanation_html: No, as the instruction results in indirect solicitation of professional work, thereby violating Clause 6 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. Clause 6 of Part I of the First Schedule prohibits a Chartered Accountant from advertising or soliciting professional work, directly or indirectly. Publishing posts on websites or social media highlighting assignments and inviting clients amounts to indirect solicitation, even if the client’s name is not disclosed. Therefore, the instruction given by CA Ankur is not in compliance with professional ethics.

questions.question_text: The presence of independent directors and constitution of Audit and Risk Management Committees indicate adherence to:

options.a: Environmental Pillar
options.b: Social Pillar
options.c: Governance Pillar
options.d: Financial Pillar

questions.explanation_html: Governance Pillar The Governance pillars include the following elements as under: • Corporate Governance: Broad Diversity, Executive Pay, Ownership, Accounting • Corporate Behaviour: Business Ethics, Anti - Competitve Practices, Corruption & Instability, Financial system and stability, Tax Transparency

title: CASE SCENARIO 23
passage_html: CA Kishan, a sole proprietor of M/s R K & Co., is a Chartered Accountant in practice. He employs CA Isha, a qualified Chartered Accountant, as a full-time paid assistant. CA Isha conducts audits, prepares reports and signs certificates under the name and supervision of CA Kishan. The firm also engages Mr. Varun, a non-Chartered Accountant, to assist in administrative coordination, client communication and liaison work. The firm pays him a portion of professional receipts described as “legal consultancy and office support charges”, although Mr. Varun does not possess any recognised professional qualification prescribed by the Council. With prior approval of the Council, CA Kishan purchases the goodwill from Ms. Vishakha, wife of a deceased Chartered Accountant. Following this acquisition, the firm witnesses a rapid expansion of its client base, including corporate and overseas clients. During this expansion phase AMC Ltd., one of the client of CA Kishan, had following cyber fraud attempts: • The CFO of a client company receives an urgent phone call from a person impersonating a bank official, requesting OTP details to reverse a supposedly failed transaction. • Around the same time, the Managing Director receives a “Highly Confidential” email appearing to originate from the Chairman, seeking immediate authorisation for an overseas wire transfer. • The attackers leveraged publicly available information and weak segregation of duties to make their communications appear authentic. Based on the above facts, answer the following:

questions.question_text: Whether payment to Mr. Varun described as “legal consultancy and office support charges” is permissible under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and the Schedules thereto?

options.a: Permissible sharing of fees due to legal consultancy
options.b: Professional misconduct under Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949
options.c: Professional misconduct under Clause (3) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949
options.d: Permissible if disclosed in the engagement letter

questions.explanation_html: Professional misconduct under Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 prohibits a Chartered Accountant in practice from sharing professional fees with a non-member, except in circumstances specifically permitted (such as sharing with members, retired partners, legal representatives of deceased partners, or persons with prescribed qualifications). Merely describing the payment as “legal consultancy” does not alter its substance. Since Mr. Varun is neither a member nor a prescribed professional, sharing fees with him constitutes professional misconduct.

questions.question_text: The phone call received by the CFO requesting OTP details to reverse a failed transaction is known as:

options.a: Whaling
options.b: Spear phishing
options.c: Vishing
options.d: Smishing

questions.explanation_html: Vishing Vishing involves fraudulent phone calls impersonating trusted entities such as banks to extract sensitive information like OTPs or passwords. The CFO receiving a call claiming to be from the bank and requesting OTP details clearly fits within vishing attacks.

questions.question_text: Whether purchase of goodwill form a non-CA in the given case will tantamount to Professional Misconduct under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and the Schedules thereto?

options.a: Purchase of goodwill from a non-CA is professional misconduct under Clause (4) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.
options.b: Purchase of goodwill from the legal heir of a deceased CA, with Council approval, is permissible.
options.c: Purchase of goodwill is permissible only if the seller is a practicing CA.
options.d: Purchase of goodwill from a non-CA amount to professional misconduct under Clause (1) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

questions.explanation_html: Purchase of goodwill from the legal heir of a deceased CA, with Council approval, is permissible. With reference to Clause (2) of Part I of First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, the Council of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India considered whether the goodwill of a proprietary concern of chartered accountant can be sold to another member who is otherwise eligible, after the death of the proprietor. It lays down that the sale is permitted subject to certain conditions discussed in the above flowchart. It further resolved that the legal heir of the deceased member has to obtain the permission of the Council within a year of the death of the proprietor concerned.

questions.question_text: The email sent to the Managing Director impersonating the Chairman and seeking urgent wire transfer authorisation is an example of:

options.a: Spear phishing
options.b: Phishing
options.c: Whaling
options.d: Smishing

questions.explanation_html: Whaling Whaling is a specialised form of phishing that targets senior executives or decision-makers (such as MDs, CEOs, or Chairpersons) with the objective of authorising high-value transactions. The impersonation of the Chairman and request for urgent wire transfer authorisation squarely qualifies as a whaling attack.

title: CASE SCENARIO 24
passage_html: M/s BAT & Co., a firm of Chartered Accountants, recently launched its official website “bat-ca.com”. The website featured bright neon colours, details of the partners, and listed some major clients with the fees charged. The website also used a “push” technology, where updates were automatically sent to subscribers without them requesting it. Around the same time, Mr. P, a partner in the firm, appeared on a business channel TV interview and handed over a bio-data of the firm to the interviewer. The bio-data contained details of: • The firm’s international affiliations. • Personal achievements and awards of Mr. P as a tax expert. • Notable clients handled by the firm. Later, another partner, Mr. Q, published a congratulatory advertisement in a leading newspaper with his photograph on the occasion of opening a new branch office. Further, M/s BAT & Co. was appointed as the statutory auditor of RST Ltd., a company covered under CARO 2020. While reporting under Paragraph 3 of CARO 2020 relating to property, plant and equipment, inventory, statutory dues, and borrowings, the audit team relied on system-generated MIS reports from the company’s ERP system, and management representations confirming the accuracy and completeness of such information. The audit team did not carry out independent verification of underlying records or evaluate the effectiveness of internal controls, on the assumption that consistency between MIS reports and management representations provides sufficient audit evidence. Based on the above facts, answer the following MCQs:

questions.question_text: Regarding the website “bat-ca.com”, which of the following statements is correct under the Council General Guidelines, 2008?

options.a: The firm is fully compliant because there is no restriction on website colours.
options.b: The firm is in violation of guidelines because it uses “push” technology and discloses client names and fees without regulatory requirement.
options.c: The website is compliant because disclosure of clients and fees is allowed on the firm’s discretion.
options.d: The firm is only liable if the website is used to actively solicit new clients.

questions.explanation_html: The firm is in violation of guidelines because it uses “push” technology and discloses client names and fees without regulatory requirement. The Council of the Institute had approved posting of particulars on website by Chartered Accountants in practice under Clause (6) of Part I of First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 subject to the prescribed guidelines. The relevant guidelines in the context of the website hosted by M/s XYZ are: • No restriction on the colours used in the website; • The websites are run on a “pull” technology and not a “push” technology; • Names of clients and fees charged not to be given. However, disclosure of names of clients and/or fees charged, on the website is permissible only where it is required by a regulator, whether or not constituted under a statute, in India or outside India, provided that such disclosure is only to the extent of requirement of the regulator.

questions.question_text: In the given case, whether approach of audit team i.e., relying on written representation and MIS with respect to reporting under relevant Standards on Auditing and CARO 2020 is appropriate?

options.a: The auditor’s approach is appropriate since consistency between MIS reports and management representations is sufficient for compliance with SAs and CARO 2020 reporting.
options.b: The auditor’s approach is acceptable as reporting largely involves matters based on information and explanations provided by management during the audit.
options.c: The auditor’s approach is inappropriate because management representations and system-generated MIS cannot substitute independent audit procedures required for compliance with SAs and CARO 2020 reporting.
options.d: The auditor’s approach is justified unless there is a specific indication of fraud or material misstatement.

questions.explanation_html: The auditor’s approach is inappropriate because management representations and system-generated MIS cannot substitute independent audit procedures required for compliance with SAs and CARO 2020 reporting. CARO 2020 reporting is an integral part of the statutory audit and requires the auditor to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence. Further, as per SA 580, “Written Representations”, management representations serve only as supplementary audit evidence, and cannot replace independent verification of records, evaluation of internal controls, and other audit procedures. Accordingly, reliance solely on MIS reports and representations—without independent verification—is not adequate for reporting and reflects non-compliance.

questions.question_text: Whether Mr. P will be held guilty for professional misconduct for handing over the firm’s bio-data during a TV interview under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and Schedules thereto?

options.a: Yes, Mr. P will be held guilty of professional misconduct under Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 because handing over bio-data promoting the firm and the partner’s achievements indirectly solicits professional work.
options.b: No, Mr. P will not be held guilty of professional misconduct as the partner did not personally read out the bio-data on TV.
options.c: No, Mr. P will not be held guilty of professional misconduct as long as the bio-data was factual.
options.d: Yes, Mr. P will be held guilty of professional misconduct under Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 only if the TV channel ran advertisements alongside the bio-data.

questions.explanation_html: Yes, Mr. P will be held guilty of professional misconduct under Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 because handing over bio-data promoting the firm and the partner’s achievements indirectly solicits professional work. Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 prohibits solicitation of client or professional work either directly or indirectly by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview or by any other means since it shall constitute professional misconduct.

questions.question_text: Whether the publishing of the photograph by Mr. Q is permissible under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and the Schedules thereto?

options.a: Yes, it is permissible as it merely conveys information about an event and does not amount to solicitation of professional work.
options.b: Yes, it is permissible since the publication highlights personal credentials of the partner and does not involve advertisement of professional services.
options.c: No, it is not permissible as it indirectly solicits professional work and promotes the partner and the firm and tantamount to professional misconduct.
options.d: Yes, it is permissible provided the publication does not contain any reference to services rendered or fees charged.

questions.explanation_html: No, it is not permissible as it indirectly solicits professional work and promotes the partner and the firm and tantamount to professional misconduct. As per Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, a Chartered Accountant in practice shall be deemed to be guilty of misconduct if he solicits clients or professional work either directly or indirectly by a circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview or by any other means.

questions.question_text: Whether the classification of advance and income recognition by Quick Trust Bank Ltd. is correct?

options.a: The bank is incorrect in not classifying the advance as NPA and in continuing to recognize interest income, since guarantees do not affect IRAC norms.
options.b: The bank is correct in not classifying the advance as NPA for provisioning purposes since the Central Government guarantee has not been repudiated, but interest income should not be recognized unless actually realized.
options.c: The bank is correct in both not classifying the advance as NPA and in recognizing interest income on accrual basis due to Central Government guarantee.
options.d: The bank should classify the advance as NPA only after 90 days of overdue irrespective of whether the guarantee is by Central or State Government.

questions.explanation_html: The bank is correct in not classifying the advance as NPA for provisioning purposes since the Central Government guarantee has not been repudiated, but interest income should not be recognized unless actually realized. If a government guaranteed advance becomes NPA, then for the purpose of income recognition, interest on such advance should not be taken to income unless interest is realized. However, for the purpose of asset classification, credit facility backed by Central Government Guarantee, though overdue, can be treated as NPA only when the Central Government repudiates its guarantee, when invoked. Since the bank has not invoked the guarantee, the question of repudiation does not arise. Hence the bank is correct to the extent of not applying the NPA norms for provisioning purpose. But this exemption is not available in respect of income recognition norms. Hence the income to the extent not recovered should be reversed.

questions.question_text: Would the auditor’s conclusion change if the advance, which has remained overdue for more than 18 months, was guaranteed by a State Government instead of the Central Government?

options.a: Yes, since the special exemption from NPA classification is not available for State Government guaranteed advances, and the account would be treated as NPA after 90 days of overdue.
options.b: Yes, but only income recognition norms would change, while asset classification would remain unaffected.
options.c: No, both Central and State Government guarantees are treated identically for asset classification and income recognition under RBI IRAC norms.
options.d: No, the account would be classified as NPA only on invocation and repudiation of the State Government guarantee.

questions.explanation_html: Yes, since the special exemption from NPA classification is not available for State Government guaranteed advances, and the account would be treated as NPA after 90 days of overdue. As per RBI IRAC norms, the exemption from asset classification applicable to Central Government guaranteed advances is not available in case of State Government guaranteed advances.
